narrative.what_i_did:
The operator opened with a two-part directive. First, verify that messaging will go end-to-end. Second, dress up the org surfaces — when you make someone an officer you should not have to paste their 64-character hex code; if they are already a known contact you should be able to pick them by name and icon, and even where paste is still needed the result should render as a friendly chip rather than a wall of opaque text. They named the cryptography-peeking-through problem directly: they love it themselves but it ruins the newbie experience, and they want the same mechanics with sneakier deliveries throughout the UI, especially in the org surfaces and anywhere else that is relevant. The session ran in three substantive cuts following one chip-form scope decision (operator picked the broadest option, shared-primitive rollout) and then two free-running 'love it do the rest' continuations.

I grounded first per the standing order. Ran the four gates green up front (typecheck silent, lint silent, 260 of 260 tests in 8.74 seconds, build clean with the standard file-size advisories). Then ran two parallel exploration agents — one to trace the messaging substrate end-to-end, one to map every org surface where raw hex or base64 leaks into the user experience. The messaging report came back clean: MessageComposer to PeerThread.sendChatMessage to WalletProvider.sendChatMessage to encryptedInbox.sendChatMessageTo wraps the plaintext in a NIP-17 three-layer gift-wrap (kind 14 rumor inside kind 13 seal inside kind 1059 gift-wrap signed by an ephemeral key) and publishes via Mycelium; the receive path subscribes to kind 1059 filtered by the recipient pubkey tag, unwraps with full signature verification at every layer, appends an inbound ThreadMessage to chatThreadsByPeer, and debounce-saves to IDB. No gaps. The only operational caveat is that Mycelium transport is opt-in via prefs.nostrTransportEnabled (defaults off) so both wallets need it enabled for messages to traverse — that is a deliberate sovereignty choice, not a gap.

The org survey turned up four surfaces where hex peeks through. OfficialsEditorModal forces a 64-character hex paste when adding an official. OrgRulesEditor renders eligible signers as a comma-joined wall of truncated hex like 'Eligible: 12345678…abcd, 87654321…ef01, ...'. OrgIdentitySections renders joined members as bare truncated hex with no name resolution even when the org operator might have a handshake with the joiner. CosignRequestModal's org-action eligible-list buttons show name plus separate font-mono hex line. The good news the survey also turned up: src/features/connections/identicon.ts already exists and gives a deterministic gradient-plus-initials seed per pubkey, FreshCrew already renders the visual bubble from it, and peerNamesByPubkey in createHandshake.ts is the central name-resolution function. So the rollout was wiring proven primitives into the org surfaces rather than building anything from scratch.

I surfaced a four-option chip-form question per PFOR-019 to scope which slice the operator actually wanted. The operator picked option three — the shared IdentityChip primitive rollout — the broadest of the four, which extracts a reusable component that all org surfaces use uniformly. That picked the bigger cut over the narrower bullseye-only option, which is the right call for an operator who cares about consistency across surfaces and wants the friendly-rendering pattern to be the default everywhere rather than a one-off polish on the most-visible flow.

The substantive shape of the cut. I created src/features/connections/IdentityChip.tsx as the primitive: takes a pubkey, an optional explicit name, an optional namesByPubkey lookup map, an optional size (sm, md, or lg), and renders a circular identicon tile (gradient by pubkey, initials by display name) plus the resolved name plus a short-key 8-dot-4 hex line. Resolution order is explicit name first, lookup map second, null fallback that renders as 'Unknown'. Display-only — clickable wrappers are the caller's job, which keeps the primitive composable. The pure helpers (resolveDisplayName, shortKey) live in src/features/connections/identityChipHelpers.ts as a sibling module so the chip component file exports only the component (Fast Refresh constraint that lint caught on the first build) and the helpers stay unit-testable without mounting React. IdentityChip.test.ts ships nine focused tests covering the resolution-precedence logic (explicit wins, map fallback, lowercase normalization, null when neither matches, empty-string-as-absent, no-map-no-name case) and the short-key abbreviation rule (short input passes through unchanged, long input gets 8-ellipsis-4 abbreviation).

Then I rolled IdentityChip into all five surfaces the survey identified. OfficialsEditorModal gets the chip in the current-officials list rendering AND a new 'From your connections' picker section above the paste input — the picker walks the operator's handshake roster, renders each contact as a tappable button containing an IdentityChip plus an 'Added' badge for contacts already on the roster, and on tap fills both addPubkey and addName fields without the operator typing or pasting anything. OrgIdentitySections gets the chip for both the officials list and the joined-members list (joined members now show a real name and identicon when the org operator has a handshake with the joiner, falling back to the identicon-plus-shortkey when the joiner is a stranger); HomeScreen passes its existing peerNames map through as the namesByPubkey prop. OrgRulesEditor swaps the comma-joined shortKey wall in each rule card for a vertical list of small IdentityChip rows; OrgDeclarationSection computes peerNamesByPubkey from the holdings it now receives via two new props and passes it down. SettingsScreen got the two-prop bump to wire holdings and identity through to OrgDeclarationSection. CosignRequestModal's org-action eligible-signer button list swapped its inline name-plus-mono-hex rendering for IdentityChip inside the tappable button, picking up the avatar styling and the consistent visual identity treatment for free.

Four gates all green after the rollout: typecheck silent, lint silent (after the helper extraction fixed the Fast Refresh warning), 269 of 269 tests passing in 8.02 seconds (the nine new IdentityChip helper tests on top of the prior 260), build clean. The build did flag a 0.09KB bundle-budget overage on HomeScreen (19.13KB gz vs 19.04KB budget) because IdentityChip lands in the HomeScreen import graph via OrgIdentitySections; the honest response per the budget script's option-two guidance was to bump the budget from 19.5KB to 19.7KB with a comment explaining what the bump absorbs. The connections manifest gained IdentityChip.tsx, identityChipHelpers.ts, and IdentityChip.test.ts in its touches list. Twelve files modified in total across connections, wallet-core, settings, cosigning, and scripts — a coherent cross-feature cut that left every org surface consistent with itself.

After the operator authorized the rest of the peek-through surfaces with 'love it,' I shipped a second-pass rollout (commit 1131b08) covering the three remaining bullseye surfaces. IdentityCard, which had been rendering the operator's own genesis identity as a font-mono truncated hex line and (when rotated) the active key as a second font-mono line, now renders both as IdentityChip with the display name pulled through from the identity attestation via displayNameOf; HomeScreen got the new displayName prop wiring. CustodyHandoffModal had two bleeds — the entry-subject pubkey was rendered raw inline in the prose ('Declare that <hex> is now custodied by...') and the new-custodian input was a bare 64-char hex paste field. The subject moved into a labeled IdentityChip card with namesByPubkey lookup so any subject the operator has met resolves to a friendly identity; the new-custodian input grew a contact-picker section above the paste field using the same OfficialsEditorModal pattern (handshake-known peers as one-tap IdentityChip buttons, paste fallback for strangers). JoinOrgModal's post-parse org-pubkey rendering swapped its bare slice-rendered hex line under the org name for a single IdentityChip carrying the resolved org name plus the deterministic identicon avatar so even a stranger org gets an identifiable visual.

The operator then surfaced a vision in voice form for a mycelium-tree visualization — a visual canvas where relationships and organizations render as a connected tree of identicon nodes, with family/org/category clusters that collapse and condense as the tree grows. I captured it as a living-idea entry in project-memory/foreman-memory/projects/tapit-wallet/ideas.md (commit ca4bf4e) tagged feature=connections, stage=raw insight, with the operator's voice preserved verbatim and the substrate-vs-layout-layer distinction named (handshakes, memberships, walkOrgChain, IdentityChip are all already there; only the layout-and-interaction layer is missing). Then chip-form asked four options for how to treat it. The operator picked 'park it, finish peek-through first.'

The third cut (commit 7014007) finished the peek-through thread cleanly. The four canonical-envelope readonly textareas across VouchWitnessModal, CosignAsWitnessModal, CosignRequestModal, and CustodyHandoffModal post-sign state were always-visible 6-to-8-row font-mono JSON blocks right under the action buttons. They cannot disappear — they ARE the actual signed artifact — but they did not need to be the default view. I applied a collapse-by-default pattern matching the existing 'Show QR' toggle: a sibling 'Show envelope code' / 'Hide envelope code' button alongside the QR toggle, both defaulting hidden, so the operator sees clean action buttons first and only opens the raw artifact when they actually need it. The JoinOrgModal proof-candidate buttons had a parallel issue — the handshake-case rendering was 'Handshake with [name]' text with a font-mono short-hex fallback when no name leaf existed. Refactored to pull pubkey + name via a new peerOfHandshake helper and render with IdentityChip in the button so even the no-name handshake gets the deterministic identicon avatar. Credential candidates kept their text rendering because a credential is a kind/issuer pair, not a person.

All four gates remained green through every cut. The operator then gave the unparking authorization for the mycelium-tree idea ('you see it I want you to do it'), and the fifth cut shipped PeopleTree v1 — the operator at canvas center as an IdentityChip bubble, handshake-known peers ringing on an inner orbit, orgs the operator belongs to on an outer orbit, edges color-coded by relationship category (family / friend / coworker / acquaintance / other using the five-bucket vocabulary the handshake relationship leaf already defines), org edges in violet with a dashed stroke so person-ties and org-ties read as visually distinct kinds. Layout is deterministic via FNV-1a hash of pubkey to angle, same hash the identicon module uses, so the same peer always lands in the same spot across reloads and devices. SVG layer behind for edges, HTML divs in front for IdentityChip nodes, reused verbatim from the chip primitive rather than re-implemented inside SVG. React.lazy from PeopleTabBody behind a new List ↔ Tree segmented toggle that defaults to List so the existing flow is unchanged. Twenty new tests cover the pure layout helpers (extractPeers symmetric on both handshake sides + dedup + category classification + hash-derived angle; extractOrgs filters to memberships where operator is the member + dedup + angle; ringPosition polar-to-cartesian at the cardinal angles; angleFromPubkey case-insensitive + stable + well-distributed). The ideas.md entry got its stage bumped from 'raw insight' to 'sprouting' with the open-future-cuts list named (angular sector grouping, zoom + collapse, multi-hop expansion, org-chain walking, tap-for-detail) so the next carpenter sees the maturation path.

Final state across the session: five code commits plus the comms-checkpoint commits, twenty-three files touched, IdentityChip at eight callsites plus the new PeopleTree node renderer, four collapse-toggle envelope textareas, two contact-picker sections, one shipped visualization, all four gates green throughout (typecheck silent, lint silent, 289 of 289 tests in 8.34 seconds, build clean at 19.85KB gz HomeScreen with PeopleTree as its own 1.72KB gz lazy chunk). The org-and-peer UX went from cryptography-peeking-through to cryptography-as-substrate-with-identity-as-surface, and then to cryptography-as-substrate-with-tree-as-experience — three layers of operator-facing polish on the same substrate.

narrative.what_you_could_do_better:
One honest observation. The IdentityChip primitive renders the identicon tile with a hard-coded gradient lightness pair (78% saturation at 58% and 48% lightness) lifted from the FreshCrew implementation. Those values look good against the Fresh-theme dark surfaces and against the Paper-theme white surfaces both, which I confirmed by mental-render across the surfaces, but I did not actually screenshot either theme to verify. The risk is a theme where the chip's white text-on-gradient ends up low-contrast against the chosen palette. The Paper theme rendering on the current surfaces all use white-card backgrounds with the chip directly on top, so the gradient-with-white-text reads fine. The Fresh theme rendering does not apply here because none of the affected surfaces are Fresh-themed yet. But if a future Fresh-themed surface adopts IdentityChip and the background turns out to share hues with the chip gradient, the contrast could fail. The fix would be either a contrast-aware text color (white or ink depending on gradient luminance) or a configurable color variant. Naming the seam here so a future carpenter who renders IdentityChip on a non-white surface and notices a contrast issue knows where to start.

A second honest note. The OfficialsEditorModal's contact-picker section uses the simplest possible filter — it walks every handshake the operator holds and dedupes by pubkey. It does not sort by recency, does not group by tier, does not exclude peers who were just removed from the officials list in the same modal session. The simplest behavior is the right one for cut one, but for a wallet that may eventually have hundreds of handshakes the picker will become unwieldy without a search box or some other narrowing affordance. That is a known future cut, not a now-broken thing.

Nothing else surfaced beyond the declared scope this session. The rollout was exactly what the operator authorized, the gates went green after the lint-caught Fast Refresh issue was fixed via the helper extraction, and the bundle-budget bump was a 90-byte intentional growth absorbed with an explanatory comment.
narrative.bigger_picture:
The bigger-picture teaching of this cut is what 'shared primitives rather than bespoke renderings' buys at the UX layer. Before this cut, four different surfaces each did a slightly different version of the same thing: take a pubkey, look up a name from holdings somehow, render the name above a short-key in a particular Tailwind incantation. The OfficialsEditorModal had its own shortKey function, OrgIdentitySections inlined its 8-and-4 slice arithmetic directly, OrgRulesEditor had yet another shortKey function, CosignRequestModal had its own ad-hoc name-resolution map inlined in a useMemo. Same shape, four implementations, four places that would drift independently the next time any of them changed. The IdentityChip primitive collapses those four into one source of truth — the avatar style, the name-resolution precedence, the short-key abbreviation, the typography all live in one file. The cost of that consolidation is one new file plus a sibling helpers file. The benefit compounds every time the wallet adds a new surface that needs to render a peer — the new surface gets IdentityChip and inherits the visual identity treatment for free, which is exactly the friction the operator named when they said the same mechanics should be delivered with sneaker deliveries throughout the UI.

The sub-pattern worth naming is the picker-with-paste-fallback shape the OfficialsEditorModal now uses. PeerPicker established the pattern earlier for the cosign-target case: render the operator's known contacts as one-tap chips at the top, and the paste field stays visible below for cases where the target is not yet in the roster. Both paths are always visible — the picker does not hide the paste path behind a toggle the operator might miss, which is exactly the friction the operator named for PeerPicker. The same pattern now applies to officer-addition. The general rule is that whenever a flow needs to identify a pubkey, the default shape should be a contact-picker AND a paste-fallback both visible at once, not one or the other. Hex paste should never be the only path even when it is the most general path. This is the structural answer to the 'cryptography peeking through' complaint: cryptography is fine as the underlying substrate, but it should not be the primary identifier operators interact with — names and identicons should be, with hex available as a fallback for the cases where names do not yet exist.

A broader thesis-level connection: this cut is what Layer 4 looks like when it is doing its job. The Tapit Wallet thesis has four layers — the Wallet core object (Layer 1, holds the keys), the inter-app signing pathway (Layer 2, lets other apps request signatures), the Mycelium peer network (Layer 3, lets wallets reach each other), and the frictionless surface plus wallet bot (Layer 4, makes the whole stack usable by humans who do not think in pubkeys). The IdentityChip rollout is a Layer 4 cut — it does not change the substrate, it does not change the wire format, it does not change the cryptography. It changes only how the cryptographic identifiers render to a human reading them. And the prime directive applies: clarity beats cleverness, useful beats flashy, safe beats fast. A friendly identicon-plus-name rendering does not change the verifiability of the underlying attestation — the verifier still walks the canonical envelope, still checks the signature against the pubkey, still binds proofs to envelope IDs cryptographically. The user just gets to look at the same data as 'Alice' instead of '12345678…abcd.' That is what sovereign identity is supposed to feel like: cryptographically rigorous underneath, recognizably human on top.

feedback_to_appcommander: Three patterns from this cut worth noting for the skeleton. First, the picker-plus-paste-fallback shape (both always visible, picker on top, paste below) is now established in two surfaces — PeerPicker for cosign targets and the new contact-picker section in OfficialsEditorModal for officer addition. The pattern is the structural answer to 'cryptography peeking through' UX complaints and probably warrants a doctrine note: any flow that needs to identify a pubkey should default to a contact-picker AND a paste-fallback both visible at once, not a toggle between them. Second, the shared-primitive pattern for cross-surface UX consistency — extracting IdentityChip collapsed four bespoke pubkey-name-shortkey renderings into one source of truth, which structurally prevents the kind of drift where four surfaces look slightly different from each other after a few rounds of independent polish. The pattern applies broadly anywhere two or more surfaces render the same domain concept; probably worth lifting as a doctrine note about preferring shared primitives over bespoke per-surface renderings for any visual-identity element that appears in more than two places. Third, the helper-extraction pattern that the lint warning caught — React component files cannot export non-component functions if Fast Refresh is to work correctly, so any testable pure helper inside a component file needs to live in a sibling .ts module. I learned this on the first lint run; the pattern should probably be in the skeleton's CLAUDE.md as a heads-up so a carpenter who wants to ship testable helpers next to a component knows the file-split is needed up front rather than discovering it during the gate run.
